title: Reaching for the next element
summary: Why looking at the next array element can go past the end, and how to stop the loop before that happens.
objectives: Explain why the last valid index of an array is one less than its length.
Trace a loop that compares each array value with the next one.
Recognize why `temps[i + 1]` fails on the last loop pass.
Fix the loop so it compares each neighboring pair without going past the array.

blocks.text: Code Coach flags this pattern. The loop visits every index in `temps`, but its body also reaches for the next index with `temps[i + 1]`.

blocks.title: The important detail
blocks.text: The loop condition allows `i` to reach the last valid index. On that pass, `i + 1` is not a valid index. Java compiles this code, but it throws an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when it runs.
An array of length 3 has three boxes. Java numbers them from 0, so their indices are 0, 1 and 2. The length is a count of boxes, not an index. Here, `temps.length` is 3, and there is no `temps[3]`.

blocks.caption: `int[] temps = {18, 21, 19};`
blocks.name: temps
blocks.note: The loop reaches `i = 2`. Then `i + 1` is 3, the gap after the last box. `temps[3]` is outside the array.

blocks.caption: The loop reaches the last index, then asks for the next one

flowchart TD

blocks.title: Think in pairs
blocks.text: To compare a value with the next value, the last useful `i` is one before the last index. For an array of length `n`, the final pair is at indices `n - 2` and `n - 1`.

sections.title: Trace it, one pass at a time

blocks.text: Trace the loop by writing down `i`, checking the loop condition, and then checking both array indices used by the body. The loop condition is still true when `i` is 2.

blocks.caption: Tracing the flagged loop with `temps.length` equal to 3
columns: What the body tries to do
rows: Read `temps[3]`; this index is outside the array, so the program throws an exception.

blocks.text: The exception happens while evaluating `temps[i + 1]`. The loop does not get to finish that pass or move on to another one. The fix is to stop before the last index becomes `i`.
First, run the flagged pattern inside a complete program. It compiles, then fails on the third pass. Because the exception happens before the final print, standard output is empty.

bad.title: Flagged loop: crashes while running
bad.error: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3

good.title: Stop before there is no next element

blocks.note: The fixed loop stops when `i` reaches 2 because `2 < temps.length - 1` is false. It compares the pairs at indices 0 and 1, then 1 and 2. Only the first pair rises. The original compiles too; its error occurs at run time, not compile time.

blocks.text: Now try a different set of values. The same fixed loop checks each neighboring pair. It does not need a special case for the last value.

blocks.title: Check the second example
items: The loop stops before `i = 3`, because there is no value after index 3.

blocks.text: The same mistake can hide in a different loop condition or in a single array access. Ask whether the code might use an index equal to the array length.

bad.title: The loop includes the last index

good.title: The loop stops before the last index

blocks.note: When `i` reaches `temps.length - 1`, the bad version still runs the body. Then `i + 1` equals `temps.length`, which is not a valid index.

bad.title: Ask for the next value after the last one

blocks.note: `temps.length` counts the boxes. It does not name the last box. The last valid index is `temps.length - 1`.

blocks.title: A useful check
blocks.text: Before reading `array[i + 1]`, ask whether the loop guarantees that `i + 1` is less than `array.length`. If it does not, the last pass can reach past the end.

blocks.question: For an array with length 4, what is the largest value of `i` that can safely be used in `array[i + 1]`?
blocks.explanation: The largest safe `i` is 2. Then `i + 1` is 3, the last valid index. If `i` were 3, `i + 1` would be 4, which is outside an array of length 4.

blocks.question: Which loop condition safely checks every neighboring pair in `temps`?
blocks.explanation: The condition `i < temps.length - 1` stops before `i` reaches the last index. That leaves a valid next element for `temps[i + 1]`.

blocks.question: What happens when this code runs with an array of length 3?
options: It prints every value and stops normally.
It fails at run time when it tries to read index 3.
It is rejected by the compiler.
It prints the final value twice.
blocks.explanation: The code compiles. On the last pass, `i` is 2, so `a[i + 1]` asks for `a[3]`. That is outside an array of length 3, so Java throws an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at run time.

items: Array indices start at 0. An array of length `n` has valid indices from 0 through `n - 1`.
`array.length` is the number of boxes, not an index you can read.
The loop `i < array.length` is safe for reading `array[i]`, but it is too long when the body also reads `array[i + 1]`.
For neighboring pairs, use a condition such as `i < array.length - 1`.
An out-of-bounds access compiles and fails at run time with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
Trace the last pass and check every index the body uses.
